title: Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage
authors: Ryan Babbush, Jarrod R. McClean, Michael Newman, Craig Gidney, Sergio Boixo, Hartmut Neven
year_and_status: arXiv v1 9 Nov 2020, v2 31 Mar 2021; published PRX Quantum 2, 010103 (2021), DOI 10.1103/PRXQuantum.2.010103
what_it_does: Perspective with an explicit break-even model. Eqs (1)-(3): T_Q = M t_Q, T_C = M^d t_C, break-even T* = t_Q (t_Q/t_C)^(1/(d-1)); Eq (4)-(5) adds Amdahl-type classical parallelism S; Eq (12) adds a Toffoli speed-up factor R. Surface-code Toffoli t_G ~ 170 us (d=30, 5.5d cycles, 1 us cycle); generic lower bound t_Q >= 17 ms (100 Toffolis) vs t_C <= 33 ns; concrete example uses Sanders et al. compiled qubitized-walk simulated annealing on N=512 SK (t_Q = 440 ms) vs a measured ~7 ns classical SA step. Tables I-II tabulate break-even M and T* for d=2,3,4, S in {1,1e3,1e6}, R in {10,100,1000}. Conclusion: quadratic speedups do not give early-FTQC advantage even with >10x faster Toffolis; quartic looks practical.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the source of our C1 budget identity (we cite it as 'adapted from Babbush et al.'), so C1 is explicitly not novel. It is primitive-level: t_C is one classical SA update, not a measured end-to-end strong comparator; it has no sample-count/variance model (sigma/e), no accuracy/confidence contract, no estimator constant k, no Monte Carlo/finance instance, no width axis and no calculator. Its Table II is a one-dimensional frontier in Toffoli rate R only. Our residual novelty vs this paper: replacing t_C*M^2 by a measured RQMC/CV/MLMC time-to-accuracy T_C(eps), a compiled option-pricing oracle, and a multi-axis frontier (depth, clock, k, width, eps) with a reusable calculator.

title: Disentangling Hype from Practicality: On Realistically Achieving Quantum Advantage
authors: Torsten Hoefler, Thomas HÃ¤ner, Matthias Troyer
year_and_status: Communications of the ACM 66(5):82-87, May 2023, DOI 10.1145/3571725 (metadata via dblp/search); arXiv v1 2 Jul 2023 read
what_it_does: Perspective. Compares one A100-class classical chip (and an ASIC) with an optimistic future FTQC (10,000 logical qubits, 10 us logical gates, all-to-all, fully parallel) via a work-depth model (Table 1: I/O bandwidth and op throughput). Table 2 inverts the quadratic/cubic/quartic crossover to give the MAXIMUM number of operations affordable per oracle call for a crossover within 1e6 s (~2 weeks): 0.2 fp16 ops, 0.003 int32 ops, 68 binary ops for quadratic speedups. Also an I/O-bandwidth argument against big-data problems. Names Monte Carlo via quantum walks, Grover search, drug design, ML among likely dead ends.
difference_from_our_paper: Table 2 is conceptually an oracle-complexity budget per call at a fixed crossover time, i.e. the same inversion as our D_max, so the 'maximum affordable oracle size' idea is pre-empted in generic form. Differences: classical side is peak chip throughput, not a measured strong application solver; oracle is abstract op counts (only mantissa multiplications charged, reversibility ignored), not a compiled oracle; no accuracy/variance model (it assumes X vs X^2 calls), no estimator constant k, no width constraint beyond the 10k-qubit premise, no finance instance and no calculator. Our contribution must be framed as the measured, instance-level instantiation of this budget with a compiled oracle.

title: The Quantum Tortoise and the Classical Hare: A simple framework for understanding which problems quantum computing will accelerate (and which it will not); published as '... When Will Quantum Computers Outpace Classical Ones and When Will They Be Left Behind?'
authors: Sukwoong Choi, William S. Moses, Neil Thompson
year_and_status: arXiv v1 24 Oct 2023; published Proceedings of the IEEE (2025), DOI 10.1109/JPROC.2025.3574102 (DOI and retitle from IEEE Xplore/ADS search listing; Xplore page not opened)
what_it_does: Economics-style framework: 'quantum economic advantage' = feasibility (enough logical qubits, from vendor roadmap extrapolation and ~1:1000 physical:logical ratio) AND algorithmic advantage (quantum complexity times a hardware speed gap beats classical complexity). Worked Grover/unstructured-search example: with a ~1e6 per-operation speed gap, threshold problem size N* ~ 1e12 (arXiv v1 Sec II.C, Fig. 3). Plots problem size vs year regions; promises a web tool (later released, see L1-T04).
difference_from_our_paper: Generic asymptotic-complexity comparison with a single scalar speed gap and a qubit-count feasibility axis; no compiled oracle, no measured classical comparator, no accuracy/variance model, no Monte Carlo/finance instance, no depth/T-throughput decomposition, no estimator constant. It does pre-empt the idea of a two-constraint (width feasibility x speed) frontier over time, so our 'frontier in width and clock' must be framed as instance-level and measured rather than conceptually new.

title: Introducing the Quantum Economic Advantage Online Calculator
authors: Frederick Mejia, Hans Gundlach, Jayson Lynch, Carl Dukatz, Andrew Lucas, Eleanor Crane, Prashant Shukla, Neil Thompson
year_and_status: arXiv v1 28 Aug 2025; preprint (no journal version established); tool at futuretech.mit.edu/quantum-economic-advantage-calculator
what_it_does: Public web calculator (MIT FutureTech with Accenture) implementing the tortoise-hare framework. Inputs: user-supplied classical and quantum runtime expressions, qubit-vs-problem-size relation, vendor hardware roadmaps or custom, gate and two-qubit gate times, physical-to-logical ratio, hardware slowdown and improvement rates, classical processor count (parallelism), connectivity penalty, cost. Outputs: minimum problem size for advantage and year of 'quantum economic advantage' (speed and cost variants). Worked examples include Grover search, Shor/RSA-2048 and TSP.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the closest pre-existing REUSABLE CALCULATOR: our 'D_max calculator' cannot be claimed as the first public quantum-vs-classical break-even calculator. Differences: it works from asymptotic complexity expressions and roadmap extrapolation, not from a measured time-to-accuracy classical table T_C(eps) and a compiled oracle's T-depth/width; it has no amplitude-estimation variance/accuracy model, no estimator constant k, and no option-pricing benchmark. Our calculator must be positioned as a domain-specific, measurement-backed instantiation (oracle depth x logical clock x k x width at fixed eps and confidence) and should cite this tool.

title: Quantum Deep Learning Still Needs a Quantum Leap
authors: Hans Gundlach, Hrvoje Kukina, Jayson Lynch, Neil Thompson
year_and_status: arXiv v1 3 Nov 2025; preprint
what_it_does: Applies the quantum-economic-advantage model to deep learning. Combines gate-speed gap, error-correction overhead and GPU parallelism/cost into an effective ~1e13 slowdown; for Grover-type sqrt(N) speedups (hyperparameter search, RL action selection) the break-even problem size solves 1e13*sqrt(x) = x, giving ~1e26, far beyond feasible sizes. Adds per-subroutine (one month) and total (one year) time limits and a logical-qubit feasibility constraint; also treats HHL, q-means and QRAM limitations.
difference_from_our_paper: Domain is ML; comparator is H100 peak FLOPs and cloud prices, not a measured application solver; quadratic speedup modelled as sqrt(N) calls with scalar slowdown, no compiled oracle, no accuracy/variance/confidence contract and no estimator constant. It strengthens the 'quadratic speedups are not enough' consensus (useful citation) but does not pre-empt a measured, compiled, finance-specific frontier.

title: Quantum Advantage in Computational Chemistry?
authors: Hans Gundlach et al. (11 authors; full list not transcribed)
year_and_status: arXiv v1 28 Aug 2025; preprint
what_it_does: Extends the Choi-Moses-Thompson framework to quantum chemistry: compares classical methods of different accuracy/cost with quantum phase estimation, including error-correction overhead, processor speed and hardware/algorithm improvement trends, and forecasts crossover years (QPE beating highly accurate classical methods on small molecules within about a decade; less accurate classical methods only in 15-20 years under favourable assumptions).
difference_from_our_paper: Chemistry and QPE (super-polynomial/exponential regimes), forecast by complexity scaling and trends; no quadratic Monte Carlo speedup, no compiled oracle for our task, no finance. Useful only as another instance of the crossover-forecast genre.

title: Applying quantum algorithms to constraint satisfaction problems
authors: Earl Campbell, Ankur Khurana, Ashley Montanaro
what_it_does: End-to-end requirements study for Grover and quantum backtracking on random k-SAT and k-colouring. Classical comparator is MEASURED: Maple_LCM_Dist (SAT Competition 2017 winner) and DSATUR run on many random instances to fit runtime scaling. Quantum side: depth-optimised compiled oracles with Toffoli/T costs, surface-code factories, physical-qubit counts, a one-day runtime cap, and three hardware regimes (Table 1: realistic/plausible/optimistic gate, measurement and cycle times; error rates). Table 2 gives upper-bound speedups versus oracle depth (1000 vs 5e5) per regime and notes speedup scales ~c^2 with oracle depth/clock. Finds up to ~1e5 (optimistic) or ~1e3 speedups, but >1e12 physical qubits in some cases, and the advantage disappears once classical decoding cost is charged.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the closest METHODOLOGICAL pre-emption outside finance: measured strong classical solver + compiled depth-optimised oracle + clock/hardware regimes + width + runtime cap, i.e. the 'measured requirements frontier' template already exists (2019) for search/backtracking. Differences: domain is combinatorial search (exponential-time, Grover over 2^n), not mean estimation; no accuracy/variance/confidence contract, no estimator constant k, no sigma/e sample model and no RQMC-type comparator whose convergence rate changes the budget; frontier is a few discrete regimes, not a continuous D_max(clock,k,width,eps) surface; no reusable calculator. Our paper must cite it as the template and claim only the Monte-Carlo/pricing instantiation.

title: Compilation of Fault-Tolerant Quantum Heuristics for Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Yuval R. Sanders, Dominic W. Berry, Pedro C. S. Costa, Louis W. Tessler, Nathan Wiebe, Craig Gidney, Hartmut Neven, Ryan Babbush
year_and_status: arXiv v1 14 Jul 2020, v2 5 Aug 2020; published PRX Quantum 1, 020312 (2020)
what_it_does: Compiles, to Toffoli counts on the surface code, the primitives of several optimisation heuristics (amplitude-amplification-style search, quantum-walk accelerated simulated annealing, adiabatic, QAOA-type, Trotterised) for SK, LABS and related cost functions, optimises the oracle circuits, and compares against classical simulated annealing per-step cost. Headline: quantum-accelerated SA would need about a day and ~1e6 physical qubits for instances classical SA handles in minutes; concludes that a heuristic with only a quadratic speedup is unlikely to win on modest surface-code superconducting processors without major QEC improvements. Its N=512 SK numbers (t_Q ~ 440 ms per update, classical ~7 ns) feed Babbush et al. 2021.
difference_from_our_paper: Pre-empts the 'compile the oracle to the Toffoli level, then compare wall-clock against a classical per-step time, then conclude quadratic is not enough' pattern for optimisation. Differences: classical comparator is per-update SA cost, not a measured time-to-accuracy for a numerical estimate; no sampling-error/variance/confidence model, no k; no frontier surface across clock/width/k; no finance or Monte Carlo integration; no calculator.

title: The Fast for the Curious: How to accelerate fault-tolerant quantum applications
authors: Sam McArdle, Alexander M. Dalzell, Aleksander Kubica, Fernando G. S. L. BrandÃ£o
year_and_status: arXiv v1 30 Oct 2025; preprint
what_it_does: Perspective (AWS) on run-time reduction for FTQC: defines an effective logical clock speed, catalogues levers (reaction-limited/time-optimal computation, parallel compilation, faster magic-state supply, transversal/QLDPC schemes, low-depth arithmetic, QROAM space-time trade-offs) and illustrates with Fermi-Hubbard estimates. Table I recomputes run times under a minimal-footprint surface-code model (1 us cycle and reaction) for many applications; the options-pricing entry (their ref [13]) is ~1e4 logical qubits, ~1e10 T/Toffoli, ~3e7 physical qubits and ~3.7 days per repetition. Sec. I-II advocate working BACKWARD from workflow time constraints to the required logical clock speed.
difference_from_our_paper: Pre-empts the general proposal to derive a required logical clock rate from an application's time budget, and already notes option pricing is days-slow at a 1 us cycle. It does not measure a strong classical comparator, does not compile a new oracle, does not compute a crossing depth against RQMC-type time-to-accuracy, and has no k/eps/width frontier or calculator. Our C7 (required clock vs dated hardware sources) should cite it as the conceptual precursor.

title: The Grand Challenge of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O'Brien, Nicholas C. Rubin
year_and_status: arXiv v1 12 Nov 2025, v3 4 Dec 2025; preprint
what_it_does: Google Quantum AI perspective proposing a five-stage pipeline for quantum applications (discovery, hard instances, real-world instance, resource estimate, deployment). States as a tenet that practical advantage within roughly two decades likely needs super-quadratic speedups, while acknowledging many problems admit quadratic speedups via amplitude amplification. Includes an early-FT compilation discussion: amplitude estimation (one deep circuit, O(G/eps) gates) versus sampling (O(1/eps^2) shallow repetitions) both require logical error ~O(eps/G). Tables of resource estimates (e.g. RSA-2048, FeMoco).
difference_from_our_paper: Consensus/perspective statement; no break-even calculation, no classical measurement, no oracle compilation for Monte Carlo. Discrepancy to resolve: the 23-Sep screening row says it places derivative pricing in the quadratic-only bucket, but a full-text term search of the v3 HTML on 2026-10-01 returned no occurrences of 'derivative', 'pricing', 'finance' or 'option'; the paper should cite it only for the super-quadratic tenet and the AE-vs-sampling logical-error point unless the finance statement is re-located.

title: Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods
authors: Ashley Montanaro
year_and_status: arXiv v1 27 Apr 2015, last revised 11 Jul 2017; Proc. R. Soc. A 471:20150301 (2015)
what_it_does: Algorithmic result: near-quadratic quantum speedup for estimating the mean of a randomized subroutine's output with bounded variance (variance-sensitive mean estimation, O~(sigma/eps) calls), with applications to partition functions via quantum walks. Asymptotic/query-level; no hardware constants, overheads or break-even analysis.
difference_from_our_paper: Supplies the O(sigma/eps) quantum sample model that our k*(sigma/e) term abstracts; it makes no practical crossover claim, so it does not pre-empt any requirements or frontier claim. Our k constant must be tied to its (and successors') theorem constants and log factors (Track L3).

title: Assessing requirements to scale to practical quantum advantage
authors: Michael E. Beverland, Prakash Murali, Matthias Troyer, Krysta M. Svore, Torsten Hoefler, Vadym Kliuchnikov, Guang Hao Low, Mathias Soeken, Aarthi Sundaram, Alexander Vaschillo
year_and_status: arXiv v1 14 Nov 2022 (dated 19 Nov 2022); preprint on arXiv (no journal reference shown on abs page)
what_it_does: Layered resource-estimation framework and the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator tool (a public, reusable estimator from logical program counts to physical qubits and runtime across qubit parameter sets and QEC schemes). Applies it to 2D transverse-field Ising dynamics, a carbon-fixation chemistry catalyst, and RSA factoring. Sec. I states practical advantage will only come for small-I/O, superquadratic (ideally exponential) speedups; lists 'requirements for scale': controllable (>1e6 qubits, <1e-3 failure), fast (sub-microsecond physical operations for <=1 month runtime at ~1e6 physical qubits), small.
difference_from_our_paper: Supplies a requirements-in-clock-speed statement and a reusable resource estimator, so neither 'required operation speed' nor 'a reusable resource tool' is new in general. It does not analyse any quadratic-speedup application, measures no classical comparator, and computes resources not break-even. Our calculator differs by computing D_max against a measured classical time-to-accuracy; we could feed our compiled oracle into this estimator as a cross-check rather than claim tool novelty.

title: A Threshold for Quantum Advantage in Derivative Pricing
authors: Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Rajiv Krishnakumar, Guglielmo Mazzola, Nikitas Stamatopoulos, Stefan Woerner, William J. Zeng
what_it_does: Finance threshold paper: compiles full AE pricing circuits (re-parameterisation loading, GBM) for an autocallable and a TARF to T-count, T-depth (~5.4e7) and ~8,000 logical qubits, and states the threshold as running the program in about a second (the classical target; per the 23-Sep screen a practitioner anecdote at 68% confidence, not a measured optimised solver).
difference_from_our_paper: This is the direct finance precedent for 'compiled pricing oracle vs a classical time target -> required T rate'. It pre-empts the idea of a pricing break-even threshold. Differences: classical side is an assumed ~1 s target, not a measured RQMC/CV/MLMC time-to-accuracy; 68% confidence; single operating point, not a frontier in depth x clock x k x width x eps; no knock-out payoff; no calculator. Our paper must present itself as a measured-comparator re-do and generalisation of this threshold, not as the first pricing threshold.

title: Derivative Pricing using Quantum Signal Processing
authors: Nikitas Stamatopoulos, William J. Zeng
year_and_status: arXiv v1 26 Jul 2023, v2 16 Apr 2024; Quantum 8, 1322 (2024)
what_it_does: Replaces payoff/exponential arithmetic with QSP amplitude encoding; reports ~16x fewer T gates, ~4x fewer logical qubits and ~5x lower required logical clock than the Chakrabarti et al. threshold; break-even stated as ~4.7k logical qubits and ~1e9 T gates executed at ~45 MHz.
difference_from_our_paper: Second finance threshold paper expressing break-even as a required T-gate rate for a compiled oracle; inherits the assumed ~1 s classical target and 68% confidence. It gives a single required-clock number, not a frontier; no measured classical comparator and no calculator. Together with L1-T13 it pre-empts 'required clock for a compiled pricing oracle' as a concept.

title: Quantifying Grover speed-ups beyond asymptotic analysis
authors: Chris Cade, Marten Folkertsma, Ido Niesen, Jordi Weggemans
year_and_status: arXiv 2203.04975 (v2 HTML read); published Quantum 7, 1133 (10 Oct 2023) per the Quantum journal listing
what_it_does: Empirical methodology: classically emulates Grover-based subroutines (search with unknown number of marked items, maximum finding) while recording rigorous expected/worst-case query bounds, then compares quantum and classical hill-climbing heuristics for MAX-k-SAT on concrete instances in query counts. Finds only part of the per-step quadratic speedup survives; only one of the quantum hill climbers attains an absolute (query) speedup at the sizes studied. Sec 1.4 deliberately stays architecture-independent (no gate counts, no QEC overhead, no clock).
difference_from_our_paper: Shares the 'measure on concrete instances rather than trust asymptotics' stance and shows the effective k-like constant erodes Grover speedups, but stops at query counts: no compiled oracle, no wall-clock, no logical clock or width, no frontier and no calculator. Useful to cite for the instance-level constant-factor argument (analogous to our k and sigma/e measurement).

title: Is Quantum Search Practical?
authors: George F. Viamontes, Igor L. Markov, John P. Hayes
year_and_status: arXiv quant-ph/0405001, 30 Apr 2004; journal version not verified (secondary listings suggest an IEEE magazine, 2005: unknown)
what_it_does: Early (pre-2020) critique of Grover applications. States requirements for quantum search to be practical: a search task where classical methods do not scale, a quantum algorithm with better asymptotic worst-case runtime than any classical algorithm, and smaller actual runtime on practical instances; argues database and many commonly proposed search applications fail these because real problems contain exploitable structure and oracle construction is costly. Uses a simulation methodology for evaluating speedups.
difference_from_our_paper: Qualitative requirements for Grover practicality, pre-fault-tolerance era; no QEC overhead, no break-even formula, no Monte Carlo, no compiled oracle or frontier. Useful as the earliest 'quadratic speedup is not enough in practice' citation, including the point that the comparator must be the best classical method on real instances (our 'strong classical comparator' checklist item).

title: Implementing Grover oracles for quantum key search on AES and LowMC
authors: Samuel Jaques, Michael Naehrig, Martin Roetteler, Fernando Virdia
year_and_status: EUROCRYPT 2020 (IACR ePrint 2019/1146 is a minor revision; received 3 Oct 2019, last revised 7 Jun 2023); arXiv 1910.01700
what_it_does: Cryptanalysis requirements study: full Q# Grover oracles for AES-128/192/256 and LowMC with automatic resource estimation, optimised for depth at the expense of width, and costed under NIST's MAXDEPTH depth caps (2^40, 2^64, 2^96). Because Grover parallelises poorly, imposing MAXDEPTH forces parallel instances and inflates gate cost and depth-times-width cost by large factors (per search-result summary: ~2^34 at MAXDEPTH 2^40); the costs define NIST security categories.
difference_from_our_paper: Establishes, for Grover in cryptanalysis, a compiled-oracle cost analysis under an explicit DEPTH budget with a depth-width trade-off and the parallel-Grover penalty, i.e. a precursor of our depth/width frontier and of the P_Q axis. It compares to classical brute-force cost only abstractly (security categories), with no measured classical comparator, no accuracy/variance model and no logical-clock mapping to wall time. Must be cited for the depth-limited Grover and parallelisation-penalty ideas.

title: Cost analysis of hash collisions: will quantum computers make SHARCS obsolete?
authors: Daniel J. Bernstein
year_and_status: SHARCS'09 Workshop Record, Lausanne, 9-10 Sep 2009; workshop paper
what_it_does: Pre-2020 price-performance comparison: shows the Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp quantum collision algorithm (nominal 2^(b/3)) has worse price-performance than classical parallel van Oorschot-Wiener collision circuits, even under optimistic assumptions on quantum speed, because cheap classical parallel hardware achieves comparable scaling at far lower cost.
difference_from_our_paper: Early instance of the argument that a modest query speedup loses to parallel classical hardware once cost/area is accounted for; cryptanalytic, no Monte Carlo, no QEC model, no compiled oracle or frontier. Useful as the pre-2020 origin of the 'parallel classical comparator erases small quantum speedups' point that our S/GPU axis relies on.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Trading: A Survey of Speedups, Thresholds, and Dequantization
authors: Luigi Laura, Marco Parrillo, Alessio Pascucci, Marco Rossi, Valerio Rughetti
year_and_status: Information (MDPI) 17(9):908, published 17 Sep 2026 (metadata from OpenAlex and DOAJ; MDPI page returned 403/Access Denied, so full text NOT read)
what_it_does: Structured critical review of quantum algorithms for trading. Per its abstract: AE gives O(1/eps) queries vs O(1/eps^2) plain-MC samples, but this does not establish end-to-end runtime advantage once state preparation, arithmetic, error correction and classical competitors are costed; published resource estimates for benchmark exotics need thousands of logical qubits and demanding logical operation rates; an ILLUSTRATIVE SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS shows how the AE-vs-classical crossover depends on classical throughput, oracle depth and the comparison window (numbers explicitly scenarios, not calibrated forecasts). Also a 250-instance portfolio benchmark where classical MIP and a heuristic win, dequantisation of low-rank QML, and a quantum-kernel equity study.
difference_from_our_paper: MOST RECENT AND CLOSEST FINANCE THREAT (two weeks old): it already publishes, for derivative pricing, a crossover sensitivity in oracle depth x classical throughput x time window and the 'query advantage is not runtime advantage' argument. From the abstract it has no measured strong classical comparator (throughput is a scenario parameter), no compiled oracle of its own, no estimator-constant k or eps/confidence contract, no width axis and no calculator; this must be confirmed by reading the full text (blocked here). Our paper must cite it and position the frontier as measured and compiled rather than illustrative.

title: Assessing fault-tolerant quantum advantage for k-SAT with structure
authors: Martijn Brehm, Jordi Weggemans
year_and_status: arXiv v1 17 Dec 2024, v3 15 Jan 2026; Quantum 10, 1975 (2026)
what_it_does: Hybrid benchmarking of quantum backtracking and Grover against the MEASURED 2023 SAT Competition main-track winner on random k-SAT with tunable structure, converting to quantum run times via both T-depth and T-count cost models and a one-day solve requirement. Reproduces Campbell-Khurana-Montanaro in the unstructured case, then finds almost all quantum speedups vanish (even asymptotically) once minimal structure is added or T-count replaces T-depth; within one day only Grover retains a narrow T-depth-only regime.
difference_from_our_paper: Current state of the art for the 'measured strong classical solver + compiled Grover-type oracle + runtime cap + cost-model sensitivity (T-depth vs T-count)' methodology, and it reaches the same negative verdict type. It pre-empts the methodological template (with L1-T07) outside finance. Differences: search/SAT rather than mean estimation, so no variance/accuracy/confidence model, no k, no RQMC-rate effect; frontier is expressed as regimes not a continuous D_max(clock,k,width,eps); no calculator. Our novelty claim must be domain transfer to Monte Carlo pricing plus the convergence-exponent mechanism (p_C) and the knock-out case, not the methodology itself.

title: Assessing Quantum and Classical Approaches to Combinatorial Optimization: Testing Quadratic Speed-ups for Heuristic Algorithms
authors: Pedro C. S. Costa, Mauro E. S. Morales, Dong An, Yuval R. Sanders
year_and_status: arXiv v1 17 Dec 2024; published 2025 with DOI 10.1103/hm1z-z9p2 per OpenAlex (APS journal page not opened)
what_it_does: Numerical benchmarking of quantum versus classical heuristics for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick problem to test whether claimed quadratic speedups exist; finds a simple classical approach matches the quantum methods studied, casting doubt on any advantage, and argues asymptotic analysis alone cannot support advantage claims.
difference_from_our_paper: Shares the stance that a strong classical comparator erases nominal quadratic speedups, in optimisation. It works at algorithm/scaling level; no FT compilation to wall-clock, no logical clock or width frontier, no Monte Carlo pricing and no calculator.

title: The prospects of Monte Carlo antibody loop modelling on a fault-tolerant quantum computer
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Anna Vangone, Agnes Meyder, Stanislaw Adaszewski, Martin Strahm, Chang-Yu Hsieh, Shengyu Zhang
year_and_status: arXiv v1 20 May 2021, v2 14 Jul 2022; Frontiers in Drug Discovery (8 Jul 2022)
what_it_does: Industrial-size resource analysis of quantum Markov-chain Monte Carlo (quantum-walk speedup of MCMC) for antibody loop modelling: proposes a dihedral-angle register encoding and a coherent MCMC update from a classical all-atom force field, and estimates fault-tolerant time and space requirements; concludes they are considerable but could become reachable with technological progress.
difference_from_our_paper: A compiled-oracle resource estimate for a quadratic (quantum-walk MCMC) Monte Carlo speedup in another domain, but framed optimistically and without a measured classical time-to-accuracy comparator, break-even frontier or calculator. Useful as a cross-domain example that coherent force-field/arithmetic oracles dominate cost, as in our pricing oracle.

title: Analyzing Prospects for Quantum Advantage in Topological Data Analysis
authors: Dominic W. Berry, Yuan Su, Casper Gyurik, Robbie King, Joao Basso, Alexander Del Toro Barba, Abhishek Rajput, Nathan Wiebe, Vedran Dunjko, Ryan Babbush
year_and_status: arXiv v1 27 Sep 2022, v3 27 Sep 2023; PRX Quantum 5, 010319 (2024)
what_it_does: Improved and fully compiled (Toffoli-level) quantum TDA algorithm with Kaiser-window amplitude estimation; shows super-quadratic speedups arise only for multiplicative-error targets with growing Betti numbers, gives a dequantisation, and identifies instances where tens of billions of Toffolis could address seemingly intractable cases, in the spirit of the 'focus beyond quadratic' programme.
difference_from_our_paper: Applies the Babbush-2021 criterion (look for super-quadratic regimes, compile constants) to TDA; no quadratic-speedup break-even frontier against a measured classical solver and no finance. Background for the 'compile constants before claiming advantage' norm.
